title: Baseline Player Profile and Testing Orientation
objective: Develop a complete starting profile for each player by combining physical information, football background, positional role, self-assessment and coach observation before formal testing begins.
groundSize: Clubrooms, meeting area and a 20 × 20 metre football area.
equipment: Scales if body-mass recording is appropriate
setup:
Prepare one profile form for every player.
Divide the form into personal information, football background, preferred positions, current roles, injury considerations, goals and self-ratings.
Establish a short football activity area where coaches can observe basic movement, kicking, handballing and communication.
Explain that the profile is a starting point rather than a selection verdict.
Protect personal and medical information and restrict access to appropriate coaching or medical staff.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete the personal and football-background sections of the profile form.
Each player identifies preferred positions, previous positions, dominant side, secondary side and current role understanding.
Players rate their confidence in kicking, handballing, marking, ground-ball work, decision making, endurance, speed and communication.
Players record one short-term development goal and one longer-term football goal.
Coaches lead a five- to ten-minute low-intensity football activity and record initial observations.
The coach meets briefly with each player to clarify goals, injury considerations and role expectations.
Completed profiles are stored as the starting reference for future tests and reviews.
Testing categories are explained so players understand how later results will be used.
coachingPoints: Present profiling as a development tool rather than a judgement exercise.
Separate demonstrated performance from confidence and self-perception.
Record the player’s current role before suggesting a future role.
Ask clear questions and avoid leading the player towards a preferred answer.
Identify injury history or movement restrictions before physical testing.
Use consistent wording and rating scales across the squad.
Record observable behaviour rather than vague impressions.
Revisit player goals after testing rather than treating the first response as final.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player’s self-rating matches visible confidence and execution.
The player’s understanding of positional responsibilities.
Communication habits during the introductory football activity.
Differences between dominant-side and non-dominant-side confidence.
Whether the player can identify a specific development goal.
Players who may require additional explanation or modified testing.

commonErrors.error: Players rate every area highly or poorly without reflection.
commonErrors.correction: Ask for one example that supports each major rating.

commonErrors.error: Coaches treat the first profile as a final judgement.
commonErrors.correction: Label all ratings as baseline information to be reviewed later.

commonErrors.error: Injury information is ignored during later testing.
commonErrors.correction: Mark required modifications clearly before testing begins.

commonErrors.error: Player goals are vague.
commonErrors.correction: Convert each goal into a specific behaviour or measurable outcome.

commonErrors.error: Coaches record personality judgements instead of behaviours.
commonErrors.correction: Write what the player did, said or demonstrated.

progressions: Add individual player interviews with line coaches.
Compare player self-ratings with coach ratings after the first testing battery.
Add leadership, communication and training-behaviour ratings.
Link every player goal to one training action and one review date.
regressions: Use a shortened profile for younger players.
Complete the form through a coach-led conversation.
Use simple three-point ratings such as developing, capable and confident.
Remove body measurements where they are unnecessary or inappropriate.
Allow parents or guardians to assist younger players with background information.
successIndicators: Complete the profile honestly and with adequate detail.
Identify at least one meaningful development priority.
Understand the purpose of future testing.
Communicate relevant injury or movement restrictions.
Describe their preferred role and current role expectations.
Apply the same questions and rating scales to all players.
Use the profile to modify later testing where required.
matchApplication: A complete baseline profile helps coaches interpret football performance in context. Test results become more useful when they are connected to the player’s role, experience, physical condition, confidence and development goals rather than being viewed as isolated numbers.
relatedDrills: TA-002 – Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test

title: Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test
objective: Measure each player’s current kicking accuracy from controlled and moving starts across short and medium distances using a repeatable testing method.
groundSize: A 40 × 30 metre area with marked kicking stations at 15, 25 and 35 metres.
setup:
Create three kicking stations at 15, 25 and 35 metres from a target gate.
Make the short target gate approximately 3 metres wide, the medium gate 4 metres wide and the long gate 5 metres wide.
Establish separate starting cones for stationary kicks and kicks after a five-metre approach.
Prepare a scoring system of two points for a kick through the gate, one point for a kick reaching the target player within one step, and zero points for an inaccurate or unmarkable kick.
Modify distances for younger or developing players while preserving the same scoring method.
Assign one recorder and one target player to each station where numbers allow.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player completes two practice kicks at the first station.
The player then performs five scored kicks from 15 metres using the preferred foot.
The player performs five scored kicks from 15 metres using the non-preferred foot.
The same sequence is completed from 25 metres.
Suitable players complete five preferred-foot kicks and five non-preferred-foot kicks from 35 metres.
Players then repeat one five-kick set from 25 metres after receiving and moving through the approach cone.
Record the score, target side, kick type and any obvious technical breakdown.
Rotate players through kicking, targeting, football return and recording roles.
Calculate accuracy percentages for preferred foot, non-preferred foot, stationary kicking and kicking on the move.
coachingPoints: Use the same ball condition, distances and target widths for every tested player.
Do not provide technical coaching during the scored attempts.
Allow a standardised warm-up before testing.
Require the target player to remain in the same position.
Record whether misses are left, right, short or over the target.
Separate accuracy from distance capability.
Ensure the player begins each repetition from the marked starting point.
Retest under comparable conditions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The difference between preferred and non-preferred foot.
Whether movement before the kick improves or reduces accuracy.
Whether the player sacrifices control when attempting greater distance.

commonErrors.error: Distances or target widths change between players.
commonErrors.correction: Measure and mark every station before testing begins.

commonErrors.error: Players receive technical feedback during scored attempts.
commonErrors.correction: Save coaching feedback until the test is complete.

commonErrors.error: Target players move to make inaccurate kicks appear successful.
commonErrors.correction: Require the target to hold the marked position.

commonErrors.error: Coaches record only successful kicks.
commonErrors.correction: Record the direction and type of every miss.

commonErrors.error: Younger players are tested from unrealistic distances.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the stations while keeping the process consistent.

progressions: Add kicks after a ground-ball collection.
Add a time limit from possession to disposal.
Add position-specific kicks such as inside-50 entries, defensive exits or corridor passes.
Conduct a separate pressure-kicking test after the baseline has been established.
regressions: Test only the preferred foot initially.
Allow a stationary ball-drop rehearsal before each attempt.
Reduce the number of scored kicks for younger players.
successIndicators: Complete the required attempts using the same routine.
Produce accurate, markable kicks at age-appropriate distances.
Show a clear and repeatable miss pattern that can guide future coaching.
matchApplication: Accurate kicking is central to retaining possession, changing angles, entering the forward line and exiting defence. The test identifies the distances, sides and movement conditions under which each player can currently execute a reliable match disposal.
relatedDrills: TA-001 – Baseline Player Profile and Testing Orientation
TA-003 – Handball Accuracy and Release-Speed Test

title: Handball Accuracy and Release-Speed Test
objective: Measure each player’s handball accuracy and release speed from stationary, moving and non-preferred-side conditions using a standardised testing sequence.
groundSize: A 20 × 15 metre area with handball stations at 5, 8 and 12 metres.
equipment: Target boards or marked target gates
setup:
Establish target stations at 5, 8 and 12 metres.
Use a target board, net or marked receiving gate approximately 1.5 metres wide.
Mark a receiving cone three metres before the handball line for the moving test.
Prepare one preferred-side and one non-preferred-side station.
Nominate a consistent feeder, timer and recorder.
Define release time as the period from secure possession to football leaving the hand.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player completes three practice handballs on each side.
The player performs ten stationary preferred-side handballs at the eight-metre target.
The player performs ten stationary non-preferred-side handballs at the same target.
The player receives a feed while moving through the approach cone and completes five preferred-side handballs.
The player repeats the moving test on the non-preferred side.
For advanced players, five handballs are completed at 12 metres.
The timer records release time for the moving repetitions.
Award two points for hitting the central target, one point for entering the receiving gate and zero points for missing.
Record accuracy, average release time, fastest controlled release and technical observations.
Rotate players through feeder, receiver, recorder and testing roles.
coachingPoints: Keep feed speed and placement consistent.
Time only repetitions where the player gains secure possession.
Do not reward fast release when the handball is inaccurate.
Record preferred- and non-preferred-side results separately.
Maintain identical target dimensions for all players.
Use the same definition of a successful handball throughout the squad.
Allow adequate recovery so fatigue does not distort the technical baseline.
Note whether the player steps towards the target or handballs across the body.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Contact point of the striking fist.
Whether the football travels with a stable flight.
Accuracy differences between stationary and moving attempts.
Release-speed differences between preferred and non-preferred sides.
Whether the player needs extra steps before releasing.
Whether rushed repetitions become throws or uncontrolled contacts.

commonErrors.error: The feeder delivers inconsistent footballs.
commonErrors.correction: Use the same feeder and a marked feeding position.

commonErrors.error: Release time is prioritised over accuracy.
commonErrors.correction: Count a timed repetition only when it meets the accuracy standard.

commonErrors.error: A throw or scoop is recorded as a valid handball.
commonErrors.correction: Apply the legal handball standard to every repetition.

commonErrors.error: Preferred and non-preferred results are combined.
commonErrors.correction: Record each side separately.

commonErrors.error: The target distance is inappropriate for younger players.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the distance while retaining the same target and scoring process.

progressions: Require the player to identify a coloured target before releasing.
Add handballs after a ground-ball collection.
Add a turn or change of direction before the receive.
Add a fatigue block before repeating the final set.
regressions: Test five repetitions per side rather than ten.
Delay release-time measurement until technique is reliable.
successIndicators: Hit the defined target area with legal handballs.
Demonstrate a measurable result on both sides.
Maintain body control while receiving on the move.
Produce repeatable performance across the test.
matchApplication: The test measures a player’s ability to release the football accurately in congestion, link with a running teammate and use either side of the body. These actions directly influence stoppage exits, overlap running, defensive releases and attacking chains.
relatedDrills: TA-001 – Baseline Player Profile and Testing Orientation
TA-002 – Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test

title: Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to judge the football and complete uncontested chest, overhead and lead-up marks from repeatable deliveries.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre area with three marking lanes.
setup:
Create three lanes for chest marks, overhead marks and lead-up marks.
Position the feeder 15–25 metres from the marking player depending on age and ability.
Mark a two-metre receiving zone for the stationary tests.
Mark a ten-metre lead channel for the moving test.
Use one consistent feeder per station where possible.
Define a completed mark as secure control without the football touching the ground.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete two practice repetitions at each station.
At Station One, each player attempts ten chest marks from controlled kicks.
At Station Two, each player attempts ten overhead marks delivered above eye level.
At Station Three, each player completes ten lead-up marks into the marked channel.
Award one point for every clean mark.
Record whether dropped marks result from poor delivery, misjudgement, hand position or loss of control.
Record the player’s first action after any dropped mark.
Advanced groups may include five marks delivered slightly left and five slightly right of the player’s starting line.
Rotate players through marking, feeding, football return and recording roles.
Calculate an overall mark-completion percentage and separate percentages for each mark type.
coachingPoints: Standardise the quality and distance of deliveries.
Exclude clearly untestable kicks and repeat them.
Record clean control rather than whether the player touched the football.
Assess ball judgement separately from hand strength.
Do not provide corrective coaching during the scored set.
Observe whether the player moves early to the drop zone.
Record recovery behaviour after dropped marks.
Modify delivery height and distance for younger players without changing the assessment purpose.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Foot movement towards the drop zone.
Whether the player marks at the highest practical point.
Body balance at the moment of contact.
Ability to maintain control through the landing.
Immediate reaction after a dropped mark.

commonErrors.error: Poor deliveries are counted as player errors.
commonErrors.correction: Repeat kicks that fall outside the defined testable area.

commonErrors.error: Feeders change distance or trajectory.
commonErrors.correction: Use marked positions and a standard delivery instruction.

commonErrors.error: A double-grab is automatically scored as a failure.
commonErrors.correction: Score the mark if the player retains legal control.

commonErrors.error: Coaches ignore movement to the drop zone.
commonErrors.correction: Record whether the player adjusted early or remained stationary.

commonErrors.error: Younger players receive footballs above a safe height.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the trajectory and shorten the delivery distance.

progressions: Add marks after a change of direction.
Add wet-football testing under safe conditions.
Add position-specific deliveries such as defensive intercepts or forward leads.
Require an immediate disposal after the mark.
regressions: Use shorter hand or kick feeds.
Test chest marking before introducing overhead marking.
Use a lighter junior football where appropriate.
Allow the player to begin moving before the delivery.
successIndicators: Move into the correct drop zone.
Complete a high percentage of testable marks.
Track the football without turning away.
Recover quickly after an unsuccessful attempt.
Produce repeatable results across marking types.
matchApplication: Reliable marking allows a team to retain possession, intercept opposition attacks, provide forward targets and control field position. The test identifies whether errors are caused by ball judgement, movement, hand position, confidence or delivery conditions.
relatedDrills: TA-002 – Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test
TA-005 – Ground-Ball Clean Collection Test

title: Football Movement and Agility Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate, change direction, carry the football and complete a controlled disposal through a repeatable football-specific agility course.
setup:
Mark a start line and a five-metre acceleration gate.
Place change-of-direction cones at 5, 10 and 15 metres.
Create one lateral cut, one 180-degree turn and one curved running line.
Position a football at the first change-of-direction cone.
Place a target gate 15 metres beyond the final turn.
Define the finish as the moment the football passes through the target gate or crosses the target line.
Provide a separate deceleration area beyond the finish.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised movement and football warm-up.
Each player walks through the course once.
On the start signal, the player accelerates to the first cone.
The player collects the football and completes the marked change-of-direction pattern.
The player performs one legal bounce in the designated section.
At the final cone, the player steadies and kicks through the target gate.
Time begins on the start signal and stops when the kick crosses the target line.
Add a time penalty for missing the target gate or failing to complete the required bounce.
Each player completes three trials with full recovery.
Record the best valid time, average time, disposal accuracy and movement observations.
coachingPoints: Use the same course dimensions for every player.
Complete a thorough warm-up before maximal trials.
Separate raw course time from time penalties.
Do not allow unsafe cutting technique to be rewarded.
Record both best time and average consistency.
Ensure the football is positioned identically for every trial.
Provide full recovery between maximal attempts.
Modify turn angles and total distance for younger players and masters footballers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Body height before each change of direction.
Foot placement and balance through cuts.
Ability to collect the football without losing speed.
Whether the player regains control before kicking.

commonErrors.error: Players begin before the official start signal.
commonErrors.correction: Use the same starting command for every attempt.

commonErrors.error: Time is recorded without accounting for missed skill actions.
commonErrors.correction: Apply the published penalty system consistently.

commonErrors.error: Players receive inadequate recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Allow two to three minutes between maximal trials.

commonErrors.error: Unsafe cutting is rewarded because it is fast.
commonErrors.correction: Mark the trial invalid where control or safety is compromised.

commonErrors.error: Course dimensions change during the test.
commonErrors.correction: Secure and remeasure cones before testing.

progressions: Add a reactive colour or direction cue.
Add a handball option at the finish.
Add a second football skill during the course.
Test after a controlled conditioning block.
Compare ball-carrying time with a no-football agility time.
regressions: Use submaximal trials for returning or older players.
Allow a handball finish instead of a kick.
successIndicators: Maintain balance through changes of direction.
Secure the football cleanly while moving.
Execute an accurate disposal after high-speed movement.
Produce consistent times across valid trials.
matchApplication: Australian football requires players to accelerate into space, change direction around pressure, carry the football and execute after movement. This test combines physical movement with football control so that athletic speed is assessed alongside functional match skill.
relatedDrills: TA-004 – Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
TA-005 – Ground-Ball Clean Collection Test

title: Coach Rating Calibration and Reliability Exercise
Player Testing Data Record and Benchmark System
Goal-Kicking Routine and Conversion Test
objective: Assess each player’s goal-kicking conversion, routine consistency and miss pattern across controlled distances and angles.
groundSize: One forward-50 area with six marked set-shot positions.
setup:
Mark six shot locations:
Two directly in front.
Two from the left side.
Two from the right side.
Use distances appropriate to the age and competition level.
Mark a standard starting point for each shot.
Position recorders behind the kicker and near the goals.
Define the permitted preparation time.
Record wind conditions before testing.
Establish a safe football-return system outside the kicking line.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a progressive goal-kicking warm-up.
Each player completes two non-scored practice shots.
The player attempts two scored shots from each marked position.
Players use their normal set-shot routine.
The recorder notes routine duration, starting line, kick type, result and miss direction.
Award one point for a goal and zero for a behind or out on the full.
Record shots falling short separately from directional misses.
Calculate total conversion and conversion by distance and side.
Record whether routine steps remain consistent after misses.
Players rotate through kicking, recording and football-return roles.
coachingPoints: Use the same shot locations for every comparable player.
Avoid technical coaching during the scored sequence.
Record the type and direction of each miss.
Note routine consistency rather than imposing one routine.
Separate distance limitations from accuracy errors.
Allow sufficient recovery between longer shots.
Test in comparable wind conditions where possible.
Use age-appropriate distances.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Change in routine after a miss.
Conversion differences by angle and distance.

commonErrors.error: Different players kick from different locations.
commonErrors.correction: Measure and mark every shot position.

commonErrors.error: Misses are recorded only as goals or behinds.
commonErrors.correction: Record left, right, short and out-on-the-full outcomes.

commonErrors.error: Coaches alter the player’s routine during testing.
commonErrors.correction: Save technical intervention until the assessment is complete.

commonErrors.error: Younger players are tested beyond their range.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce distance while preserving comparable angles.

commonErrors.error: Wind changes are ignored.
commonErrors.correction: Record conditions and avoid direct comparison across significantly different sessions.

progressions: Add a shot after a short lead and mark.
Include a snap set shot where competition rules and player role make it relevant.
Test after a controlled running effort.
Compare practice conversion with match conversion.
regressions: Widen the acceptable target for younger players.
Complete the test over two sessions.
successIndicators: Convert at an age- and role-appropriate rate.
Reset their process after an unsuccessful shot.
Maintain conversion from both sides of the ground.
matchApplication: Set-shot conversion directly affects scoreboard outcomes. The test helps coaches distinguish technical errors, range limitations, angle-specific difficulties and routine breakdowns under repeated scoring demands.
relatedDrills: TA-002 – Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test
TA-011 – Short-Kick Decision and Execution Test

title: Contested Marking Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to establish position, judge the football and complete or neutralise a controlled one-on-one marking contest.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre area with two marking lanes.
setup:
Create two marking lanes approximately 25 metres long and eight metres wide.
Place one attacker and one defender inside each lane.
Position a consistent kicker at the delivery cone.
Mark a legal contest zone.
Establish clear body-contact and safety rules.
Pair players by size, age and experience.
Prepare scoring criteria for win, neutral result and loss.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker and defender begin side by side or in a nominated front-and-back position.
On the coach’s signal, both players move into the contest zone.
The kicker delivers a high, testable football.
The attacker attempts to mark while the defender contests legally.
Award two points for a clean contested mark, one point for bringing the football to ground and retaining or neutralising the contest, and zero points for losing the contest clearly.
Each player completes five repetitions as attacker and five as defender.
Alternate starting positions and delivery sides.
Record body position, flight judgement, contact legality and contest outcome.
Stop any repetition where the delivery creates unsafe contact.
Rotate pairs and feeders after the set.
coachingPoints: Pair players appropriately.
Use controlled, legal body contact.
Deliver footballs that create genuine but safe contests.
Record positioning and judgement, not only the final mark.
Separate attacking and defensive results.
Stop players from holding, pushing in the back or making front-on contact.
Allow recovery between repetitions.
Record how the player responds when the football reaches ground level.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to neutralise a lost aerial position.

commonErrors.error: Players are paired with major size or experience differences.
commonErrors.correction: Match players according to physical and football capability.

commonErrors.error: Poor deliveries create dangerous collisions.
commonErrors.correction: Use trained kickers and repeat untestable deliveries.

commonErrors.error: Only completed marks are assessed.
commonErrors.correction: Record positioning, contest neutralisation and recovery.

commonErrors.error: Illegal contact is rewarded.
commonErrors.correction: Mark the repetition invalid and reinforce legal technique.

commonErrors.error: Too many repetitions cause technique to deteriorate.
commonErrors.correction: Limit sets and provide adequate recovery.

progressions: Add a second defender or supporting crumber.
Add a short lead before the contest.
Add immediate disposal after a completed mark.
regressions: Replace aerial contests with protected marking.
Use a pad rather than a live opponent.
successIndicators: Establish or challenge for effective body position.
Complete or neutralise a high proportion of contests.
React immediately when the football reaches ground level.
matchApplication: Contested marking affects forward targets, defensive intercepts, wing contests and stoppage exits. This assessment identifies whether a player’s contest performance is limited by positioning, judgement, timing, hand strength or recovery.
relatedDrills: TA-004 – Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
TA-005 – Ground-Ball Clean Collection Test

title: Technical Assessment Review Circuit
objective: Complete a structured review circuit that confirms technical testing results across the first twenty Testing and Assessment records and identifies individual priorities for the next development phase.
groundSize: Half an oval divided into six to eight assessment stations.
setup:
Select six to eight stations appropriate to the squad:
Short-kick decision and execution.
Long-kick distance and accuracy.
Goal-kicking conversion.
Contested marking.
Spoiling direction.
Tackling technique.
Ruck accuracy or stoppage-role execution.
Defensive transition.
Prepare standard instructions and scoring sheets at each station.
Assign trained staff to all contact and tactical stations.
Divide the squad into balanced groups.
Establish rotation and recovery periods.
Prepare non-contact alternatives for modified players.
Confirm that previous baseline results are available for comparison.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised 15-minute warm-up.
The testing coordinator explains all station rules and scoring procedures.
Groups begin at assigned stations.
Each station operates for eight to twelve minutes.
Players complete the published attempts without technical coaching during scored repetitions.
Station coaches record raw results and observable behaviours.
Groups rotate on the central signal.
Contact stations are completed only under direct qualified supervision.
Players receive a recovery break before transition or stoppage testing.
All records are returned to the central data point.
Results are checked against previous baselines.
Each player is assigned one confirmed strength, one priority technical skill and one next-step training action.
coachingPoints: Select stations relevant to the age and role of the squad.
Use identical scoring standards across groups.
Compare results with previous tests rather than relying only on squad rankings.
Do not combine unrelated measures into one overall player score.
Record modified tests clearly.
Prioritise safety at contact and maximal-effort stations.
Provide enough recovery for reliable performance.
Link every identified weakness to a practical training response.
Confirm unusual results before reporting them.
Provide balanced feedback.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Differences between isolated technique and pressure performance.
Technical breakdown under speed or contact.
Whether previous development priorities have improved.
Whether testing results lead to clear coaching actions.

commonErrors.error: Every squad completes identical stations regardless of age or role.
commonErrors.correction: Select appropriate stations while preserving standardised scoring.

commonErrors.error: Results are combined into one total ranking.
commonErrors.correction: Review each skill and tactical measure separately.

commonErrors.error: Players receive coaching during scored attempts.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the assessment before providing feedback.

commonErrors.error: Contact stations operate without adequate supervision.
commonErrors.correction: Assign qualified coaches and enforce safety rules.

commonErrors.error: Previous baseline results are unavailable.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm records before the review session.

commonErrors.error: Results are collected without follow-up action.
commonErrors.correction: Assign a specific development priority and training response.

progressions: Compare fresh and fatigued technical performance.
Add coach and player self-rating comparisons.
Conduct the circuit at multiple points across the season.
regressions: Split the circuit across two sessions.
Replace tactical games with controlled decision drills.
Compare players only with their own prior baseline.
successIndicators: Complete valid assessments across relevant skill areas.
Demonstrate measurable strengths and development needs.
Convert findings into individual and squad training plans.
matchApplication: The review circuit brings together technical, contest and tactical assessments so coaches can understand how each player performs across the major demands of Australian football. It provides a controlled checkpoint before moving into more advanced testing, pressure assessment and role-specific evaluation.

title: Ten-Metre Acceleration and Football Collection Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate over ten metres, collect a football cleanly at speed and complete an effective disposal without losing movement efficiency.
setup:
Mark a starting line and a ten-metre timing line.
Position a stationary football at the eight-metre point.
Place a two-metre-wide handball target five metres beyond the timing line.
Establish a safe deceleration zone beyond the target.
Use the same football position and target dimensions for every player.
Prepare separate recording columns for sprint time, collection quality and disposal accuracy.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised acceleration and ground-ball warm-up.
Each player receives one walk-through and two practice attempts.
The player begins in a balanced two-point stance behind the starting line.
On the signal, the player accelerates towards the football.
The player collects the football without stopping and continues through the ten-metre timing line.
After crossing the timing line, the player handballs through the target gate.
Timing begins on the start signal and ends when the player’s torso crosses the ten-metre line.
Record the sprint time, whether the collection was clean and whether the handball was accurate.
Each player completes three valid attempts with two minutes of recovery.
Record the fastest valid attempt and the average of all valid attempts.
coachingPoints: Use an identical starting command for every player.
Require the player to begin completely behind the line.
Position the football consistently.
Separate acceleration time from skill-quality scoring.
Do not count a fumbled collection as a clean attempt.
Allow enough recovery for maximal acceleration.
Observe whether players lower their body effectively without overstriding.
Stop the test if the surface becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the football is secured in one action.
Ability to continue accelerating after collection.
Handball accuracy after the timed effort.

commonErrors.error: The player slows excessively before collecting.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage shorter final steps while maintaining forward momentum.

commonErrors.error: The football changes position between attempts.
commonErrors.correction: Mark the exact placement point and reset it after every repetition.

commonErrors.error: Timing continues through the disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Stop timing at the ten-metre line and score disposal separately.

commonErrors.error: Players receive insufficient recovery.
commonErrors.correction: Provide approximately two minutes between maximal attempts.

commonErrors.error: A fumble is ignored because the sprint time is fast.
commonErrors.correction: Mark the collection component unsuccessful and preserve the raw sprint time separately.

progressions: Begin from a prone or lateral position.
Compare the result with a ten-metre sprint without a football collection.
regressions: Begin the player closer to the football.
successIndicators: React promptly to the start signal.
Maintain speed through the timing line.
Complete an accurate disposal after acceleration.
matchApplication: Players frequently accelerate towards loose footballs before collecting and releasing under pressure. This test identifies whether a player can combine first-step speed with clean possession rather than producing speed only in a football-free sprint.
relatedDrills: TA-005 – Ground-Ball Clean Collection Test
TA-006 – Football Movement and Agility Test

title: Twenty-Metre Sprint and Ball-Carry Test
primarySkill: Sprint speed while carrying the football
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate and maintain speed over twenty metres while securely carrying and legally bouncing the football.
setup:
Mark a start line, ten-metre split and twenty-metre finish line.
Mark a bounce zone between eight and twelve metres.
Provide a fifteen-metre deceleration area beyond the finish.
Use timing gates where available.
Prepare separate result columns for total time, ten-metre split, bounce validity and ball security.
Ensure the running surface is level and dry.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a sprint and bouncing warm-up.
Each player performs one walk-through and two progressive runs.
The player begins behind the starting line holding the football.
On the signal, the player accelerates through the lane.
The player must complete one legal bounce inside the marked bounce zone.
The player continues at maximum controlled speed through the twenty-metre finish.
Record the ten-metre split and total twenty-metre time.
Mark the trial invalid if the bounce occurs outside the zone or possession is lost.
Each player completes three valid attempts with full recovery.
Record the fastest valid time and the variation between attempts.
coachingPoints: Require players to run through the finish rather than slowing early.
Use the same football size and condition for all comparable players.
Do not allow the football to be thrown forward and regathered.
Separate speed from bounce validity.
Provide two to three minutes of recovery.
Record whether the football changes the player’s normal running action.
Use a generous deceleration area.
Modify intensity for returning and masters players.

commonErrors.error: Players slow before bouncing.
commonErrors.correction: Practise placing the bounce slightly in front while maintaining stride.

commonErrors.error: The bounce occurs outside the marked zone.
commonErrors.correction: Mark the attempt invalid and repeat after recovery.

commonErrors.error: Players slow before the finish line.
commonErrors.correction: Place a run-through cone beyond the timing gate.

commonErrors.error: Footballs differ in size or inflation.
commonErrors.correction: Use standardised footballs for all trials.

commonErrors.error: Too many maximal runs are completed.
commonErrors.correction: Limit the test to three valid attempts.

progressions: Require the football to be carried in the non-preferred hand.
Add a disposal after the finish.
Compare ball-carry and no-football sprint times.
regressions: Reduce the distance to fifteen metres.
Allow a shorter approach for younger players.
successIndicators: Complete a legal bounce without major speed loss.
matchApplication: Players often carry the football at high speed while breaking lines, transitioning from defence or attacking open space. The test identifies whether ball carrying and bouncing significantly reduce a player’s running speed or control.
relatedDrills: TA-006 – Football Movement and Agility Test
TA-021 – Ten-Metre Acceleration and Football Collection Test

title: Vertical Jump and Aerial Reach Assessment
objective: Measure each player’s standing and running aerial reach while assessing safe take-off, flight control and landing technique.
equipment: Vertical jump measuring device or marked wall
setup:
Establish a standing-reach measurement station.
Mark a safe standing vertical-jump area.
Create a five-metre running approach.
Position a suspended football or reach target where available.
Ensure the landing surface is level and clear.
Record preferred take-off leg.
Prepare separate records for standing reach, standing jump reach and running jump reach.
howTheDrillWorks:
Measure each player’s standing reach with feet flat.
The player completes two practice jumps.
The player performs three standing vertical jumps.
Record the highest valid reach.
The player then completes three running jumps from a standard five-metre approach.
Record the highest running-jump reach.
Calculate standing-jump height and additional reach gained from the running approach.
Record take-off leg, arm used and landing quality.
Repeat any attempt affected by equipment movement.
Stop testing if landing control deteriorates.
coachingPoints: Measure standing reach accurately.
Require the same approach distance.
Record reach rather than relying only on device-generated jump height.
Observe landing mechanics.
Allow full recovery.
Do not permit contact with walls or equipment that alters the result.
Use a football target for role-specific interpretation.
Modify maximal jumping volume for younger and masters players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Difference between standing and running performance.

commonErrors.error: Standing reach is measured inconsistently.
commonErrors.correction: Use the same posture and full arm extension for every player.

commonErrors.error: Players use different approach lengths.
commonErrors.correction: Mark a fixed running start.

commonErrors.error: Landing quality is ignored.
commonErrors.correction: Record balance and joint alignment after each attempt.

commonErrors.error: Too many jumps are completed.
commonErrors.correction: Limit testing to three valid attempts per condition.

commonErrors.error: Reach and jump height are confused.
commonErrors.correction: Record both raw reach and calculated jump difference.

progressions: Add a football mark at maximum reach.
Test jumps from both take-off legs.
Use video to assess take-off and landing.
regressions: Replace maximal jumping with technique observation.
successIndicators: Reach effectively at the highest point.
matchApplication: Aerial reach affects marking, spoiling and ruck contests. Measuring reach and movement quality helps distinguish jumping capacity from ball judgement, positioning and contested technique.
relatedDrills: TA-004 – Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
TA-014 – Contested Marking Assessment

title: Closing-Speed and Pressure Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to close space rapidly, reduce speed under control and apply effective disposal pressure without over-committing.
setup:
Position the ball carrier at one end of the lane.
Position the defender ten metres away.
Place a disposal target fifteen metres beyond the ball carrier.
Mark a one-and-a-half-metre control zone around the ball carrier.
Restrict the defender to pressure, corralling or smothering actions without tackling.
Define a legal pressure result.
Prepare scoring criteria for close speed, control, pressure and recovery.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins stationary with the football.
On the signal, the defender accelerates towards the carrier.
The carrier may begin moving or prepare to dispose.
The defender must close space and enter the control zone without making illegal contact.
The carrier attempts to kick through the target gate.
Award the defender two points for forcing an inaccurate disposal or legal smother.
Award one point for closing under control and reducing the carrier’s available space.
Award zero points for over-running, losing balance or failing to affect the disposal.
Each defender completes six repetitions from varied starting angles.
Record closing time, body control and disposal-pressure outcome.
coachingPoints: Reward control rather than reckless speed.
Observe the defender’s final three steps.
Require hands and body position appropriate to the disposal threat.
Do not allow front-on contact into a kicking player.
Vary approach angles.
Use consistent ball carriers.
Record whether the defender can remain involved after the disposal.
Provide recovery between maximal approaches.

commonErrors.error: Defenders sprint past the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce shorter final steps and balanced control.

commonErrors.error: Excessive contact is used to affect the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and apply non-contact pressure rules.

commonErrors.error: Closing time is the only measure.
commonErrors.correction: Score control and disposal effect separately.

commonErrors.error: The carrier disposes before the defender can reasonably close.
commonErrors.correction: Standardise the release cue or minimum preparation period.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stop after the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Require a recovery movement towards the next contest.

progressions: Add a handball or sidestep choice.
Begin the carrier on the move.
regressions: Conduct the test at submaximal speed.
successIndicators: Maintain control in the final approach.
Recover into the next defensive action.
matchApplication: Effective pressure requires defenders to arrive quickly without running past the contest or conceding an easy evasion. This test identifies whether closing speed transfers into controlled and useful defensive pressure.
relatedDrills: TA-016 – Tackling Technique and Pressure Assessment
TA-019 – Defensive Transition Response Test

title: Return-to-Training Football Readiness Screen
objective: Provide a staged football-specific screen to help qualified medical, rehabilitation and coaching staff determine whether a returning player is ready to resume modified or full football training.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre rehabilitation and testing area.
equipment: Rehabilitation equipment as directed by medical staff
physicalLoad: 2–4 – Low to High according to approved stage
setup:
Confirm medical or rehabilitation approval before testing.
Review the player’s current restrictions.
Prepare five progressive stages:
Low-speed movement.
Straight-line acceleration.
Deceleration and direction change.
Football collection and disposal.
Position-specific movement.
Establish stop criteria for pain, instability, altered movement or reduced confidence.
Record the player’s pre-test symptom and confidence rating.
Ensure qualified staff supervise the screen.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player reports current symptoms, confidence and restrictions.
The player completes low-speed running and basic football handling.
If symptom-free and approved, the player progresses to controlled accelerations.
The player completes planned deceleration and change-of-direction movements.
Football collections, handballs and short kicks are introduced.
The player completes a limited position-specific pattern.
Staff assess movement quality, symptoms and confidence after each stage.
Testing stops immediately if defined concerns appear.
The player completes a post-test symptom and confidence report.
Medical and coaching staff determine the next permitted training level.
coachingPoints: This screen does not replace medical clearance.
Progress only through approved stages.
Do not pressure a player to continue.
Compare movement with the player’s normal pattern and previous results.
Record symptoms before, during and after testing.
Assess confidence as well as physical completion.
Avoid contact until separately approved.
Communicate the outcome clearly to all relevant staff.

commonErrors.error: Coaches use the screen without medical approval.
commonErrors.correction: Require documented clearance before testing.

commonErrors.error: Players skip directly to maximal movement.
commonErrors.correction: Progress through each approved stage.

commonErrors.error: Pain or instability is minimised.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the test and refer to qualified staff.

commonErrors.error: Only physical completion is considered.
commonErrors.correction: Record movement quality, symptoms and confidence.

commonErrors.error: Passing the screen is treated as match clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Use it only to guide the next training stage.

progressions: Progress to contact testing only after separate approval.
regressions: Return to rehabilitation exercises directed by medical staff.
successIndicators: Move with appropriate control and symmetry.
Meet criteria agreed by qualified staff.
matchApplication: A player must tolerate football-specific running, stopping, turning and skill execution before returning to normal training demands. This screen supports staged progression while keeping medical judgement central.
relatedDrills: TA-006 – Football Movement and Agility Test
TA-024 – Deceleration and Re-Acceleration Test

title: Physical and Football Performance Assessment Review
Match Involvement and Action Coding Assessment
Intercept Reading and Defensive Positioning Assessment
objective: Assess each defender’s ability to read play, position between the football and goal, intercept or spoil, and initiate a controlled defensive exit.
setup:
Mark an attacking entry zone and a defensive intercept zone.
Place two attacking targets inside the defensive area.
Position two defenders between the targets and goal.
Place two defensive exit gates on the wings.
Assign a kicker and supporting attacking players outside the zone.
Prepare assessment categories for starting position, scanning, intercept decision, contest execution and exit.
Use controlled contact rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers circulate the football outside the entry zone.
Defenders adjust their position according to the football and attacking targets.
On the coach’s cue, the attackers deliver into the defensive area.
Defenders decide whether to intercept mark, spoil, cover the dangerous target or support a teammate.
If possession is won, defenders attempt to exit through a wing gate.
Play continues for six seconds after the initial contest.
Observers rate defender positioning before the kick, contest decision and exit action.
Each defensive pair completes eight to twelve entries.
Attackers vary the entry angle and target.
Defenders rotate roles and partners.
Clearly untestable entries are repeated.
Video may be used to review starting position and decision timing.
coachingPoints: Observe the defender before the kick is delivered.
Assess positioning relative to ball, opponent and goal.
Reward correct decisions even when execution is imperfect.
Distinguish intercept opportunities from situations requiring a spoil.
Record communication between defenders.
Continue assessment into the defensive exit.
Avoid predictable entry patterns.
Apply legal contest rules.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Movement as the football changes sides.
Decision to mark, spoil or hold position.
First disposal after possession is won.

commonErrors.error: Assessment begins only when the kick is delivered.
commonErrors.correction: Record positioning throughout the attacking build-up.

commonErrors.error: Every defender is expected to attack the intercept.
commonErrors.correction: Assess role balance and dangerous-space protection.

commonErrors.error: Poor attacking kicks inflate defensive results.
commonErrors.correction: Repeat untestable entries.

commonErrors.error: Winning the football ends the repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Continue into the defensive exit.

commonErrors.error: Communication is not recorded.
commonErrors.correction: Include early calls and teammate organisation in the rating.

progressions: Add live forward pressure after interception.
regressions: Use one attacker and one defender.
matchApplication: Intercept defenders must read play before the football is kicked. Positioning, judgement and communication determine whether they can attack the football without exposing dangerous space behind them.
relatedDrills: TA-004 – Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
TA-015 – Spoiling Direction and Recovery Test

title: Forward Involvement and Scoring Impact Assessment
Player Self-Rating and Coach-Rating Alignment Review
Tactical Role Compliance and Adaptability Assessment
Kick-In Structure and Defensive Exit Assessment
Centre-Bounce Connection and Clearance Assessment
objective: Assess the ability of rucks, midfielders and connected players to execute centre-bounce roles and convert the initial contest into an effective clearance or defensive response.
groundSize: Centre square extending approximately forty metres in each direction.
setup:
Create two centre-bounce units with one ruck and nominated midfield roles.
Position connected wing, half-forward and half-back players outside the centre square.
Mark attacking and defensive exit gates.
Define legal contact and centre-bounce rules.
Prepare role-specific criteria for ruck, inside midfielder, defensive midfielder, outside release and connected players.
Assign observers to individual roles.
Use a consistent ball-up or throw-up process.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin in assigned centre-bounce positions.
The coach restarts play from the centre.
Teams compete to win the initial hit-out and clearance.
Play continues for eight to ten seconds after the first possession.
A successful attacking phase requires the football to pass through the attacking gate under control.
A defensive success includes winning possession, forcing a neutral stoppage or preventing a clean opposition exit.
Complete six centre bounces before changing selected roles.
Use varied ruck-hit plans and starting relationships.
Observers assess starting position, role execution, communication, contest action and post-clearance movement.
Ruck and midfield results are recorded separately and as a connected unit.
Complete at least two blocks against different opposition setups.
Video may be reviewed to confirm blocking and movement timing.
coachingPoints: Assess the connection between ruck and midfielders.
Record role execution rather than clearances alone.
Observe starting positions before the ball is in motion.
Include blocking, protection and defensive accountability.
Continue play beyond first possession.
Assess outside players who support the clearance.
Apply legal contact rules.
Avoid evaluating the ruck solely by total hit-outs.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Connection to players outside the square.

commonErrors.error: Only the clearance winner is rated positively.
commonErrors.correction: Assess blocking, pressure, protection and defensive role execution.

commonErrors.error: Play stops after first possession.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the exit or defensive response.

commonErrors.error: Ruck results are separated from midfield movement.
commonErrors.correction: Record both individual and unit connection.

commonErrors.error: Illegal holding is ignored.
commonErrors.correction: Stop and repeat the contest under legal-contact rules.

commonErrors.error: Every repetition uses the same hit plan.
commonErrors.correction: Vary the intended hit zone and opposition structure.

progressions: Add full forward and defensive structures.
Begin with an unexpected hit-zone call.
regressions: Use three midfielders without outside connections.
Stop after the first effective clearance.
successIndicators: Connect with players outside the contest.
Defend effectively after losing the clearance.
matchApplication: Centre bounces create immediate scoring and defensive consequences. This assessment measures the connection between the ruck, inside midfielders and surrounding structure rather than relying only on raw clearance totals.
relatedDrills: TA-017 – Ruck Hit-Zone Accuracy Test
TA-018 – Stoppage Role Execution Assessment

title: Team Defensive Structure and Rotation Assessment
Full-Phase Transition Chain Assessment
objective: Assess whether players can connect defence, transition, forward entry and turnover response across a complete football phase.
groundSize: Full oval or a long three-quarter-ground area.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams with full positional structure.
Begin each repetition from an opposition attack inside 50.
Assign observers to defensive, midfield and forward lines.
Prepare phase-assessment categories:
Defensive contest.
Possession win.
First exit.
Running support.
Midfield connection.
Forward entry.
Score creation.
Forward pressure.
Defensive reset after turnover.
Establish match-like contact and safety rules.
Use video where possible to capture the complete field.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession outside the opposition defensive 50.
The defending team attempts to win possession or force a turnover.
When possession changes, the defending team immediately attacks the opposite end.
Play continues through defensive exit, midfield transition and forward entry.
If the new attacking team scores, the repetition ends.
If possession turns over again, play continues until one team scores, exits cleanly or the time limit expires.
Each repetition lasts a maximum of forty-five seconds.
Teams reset to the original starting phase.
Complete eight to twelve full-phase repetitions.
Vary the initial attacking side and method of entry.
Observers score each phase separately and record where the chain breaks down.
Individual and unit results are reviewed after the activity.
coachingPoints: Assess every phase rather than only the final score.
Observe the first movement after possession changes.
Record whether players create width, depth and forward support.
Assess the balance behind the football.
Continue after secondary turnovers.
Identify the exact phase where structure or execution fails.
Use realistic time limits.
Provide sufficient recovery between high-intensity blocks.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: First disposal after possession is won.
Running support from behind and ahead.

commonErrors.error: Only the final score is used to judge the repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Rate each transition phase separately.

commonErrors.error: The activity stops after a secondary turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Continue until the phase reaches its defined end.

commonErrors.error: Players sprint forward without defensive balance.
commonErrors.correction: Record support ahead and protection behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Observers follow the football and miss line movement.
commonErrors.correction: Assign observers to specific lines or roles.

commonErrors.error: Repetitions are too long and become unstructured.
commonErrors.correction: Apply a clear phase time limit and reset rule.

progressions: Link observations with GPS or running data.
regressions: Provide the transitioning team with numerical advantage.
Stop after the first forward entry.
successIndicators: Secure and use the first disposal effectively.
Protect the ground behind attacking play.
matchApplication: Australian football is played through connected phases rather than isolated drills. This assessment identifies where a team’s transition chain succeeds or fails from defensive possession through to scoring opportunity and defensive reset.
relatedDrills: TA-019 – Defensive Transition Response Test
TA-038 – Off-Ball Work-Rate Observation Assessment
TA-050 – Integrated Match Performance Assessment Battery

title: Individual Development Plan Validation Review
objective: Determine whether each player’s current individual development plan is supported by testing, training and match evidence and update the plan with clear, achievable actions.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: Full Squad through individual reviews Maximum: Multiple Squads
groundSize: Private meeting area with an optional football area for practical verification.
setup:
Collect the player’s current development plan.
Gather relevant technical, physical, tactical and match-assessment evidence.
Review the original goals, actions and review dates.
Ask the player to complete a short self-assessment before the meeting.
Identify goals that have been achieved, progressed, unchanged or invalidated by new evidence.
Prepare a private review setting.
Limit the revised plan to a manageable number of priorities.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player explains their current development goals.
The coach reviews the original actions and expected outcomes.
The player presents their view of progress.
Testing, training, match and video evidence is compared with the original baseline.
Each current goal is classified as achieved, progressing, unchanged, unsuitable or no longer relevant.
Coaches and players identify the reason for success or limited progress.
Existing goals are retained, modified or replaced.
No more than two primary development priorities are selected.
Each priority receives a specific training action, responsible person and review date.
Success measures are defined in observable terms.
The player confirms understanding and commitment.
The updated plan is stored securely and shared with relevant coaching staff.
coachingPoints: Use multiple evidence sources.
Ask the player to reflect before giving the coach’s conclusion.
Distinguish lack of progress from an unsuitable goal or intervention.
Avoid changing goals because of one poor performance.
Limit the number of priorities.
Make actions specific and achievable.
Include player strengths.
Set a defined review date.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Areas where testing and match performance disagree.
Whether revised goals match the player’s role.

commonErrors.error: Goals are changed without reviewing evidence.
commonErrors.correction: Compare baseline, current results and observed behaviour first.

commonErrors.error: Players receive a long list of weaknesses.
commonErrors.correction: Limit the plan to one or two primary priorities.

commonErrors.error: Lack of progress is blamed entirely on effort.
commonErrors.correction: Review the quality, opportunity and suitability of the intervention.

commonErrors.error: Goals are vague.
commonErrors.correction: Define observable behaviours, actions and review dates.

commonErrors.error: The player has no voice in the review.
commonErrors.correction: Require self-assessment and discussion before finalising the plan.

progressions: Link plans with selection and role-development pathways.
regressions: Include parent or guardian support for younger players.
Compare only with the player’s own baseline.
successIndicators: Know how success will be measured.
Know when the plan will be reviewed.
Communicate the plan to relevant staff.
matchApplication: Testing and assessment should lead to improved football performance rather than remain as stored data. This review confirms that development goals remain relevant, evidence-based and connected to each player’s role.
relatedDrills: TA-001 – Baseline Player Profile and Testing Orientation
TA-009 – Player Testing Data Record and Benchmark System
TA-047 – Player Self-Rating and Coach-Rating Alignment Review

title: Testing and Assessment Chapter Final Assessment
objective: Complete a final integrated assessment that verifies player performance across technical, physical, tactical and match demands while evaluating the reliability and practical value of the club’s testing system.
groundSize: Full oval, half-oval testing stations and a private player-review area.
time: Two to three hours across one extended session or two separate sessions
setup:
Review the complete Testing and Assessment chapter and select age- and role-appropriate measures.
Establish four assessment components:
Technical skill verification.
Football-specific physical and movement testing.
Tactical and positional assessment.
Integrated match-performance simulation.
Assign trained staff to every testing and observation responsibility.
Calibrate all coaches before testing.
Prepare clear scoring, validity and modification rules.
Divide the squad into balanced testing groups.
Establish recovery periods and medical oversight.
Prepare video coverage and a central data-control point.
Ensure individual development plans and previous baseline results are available.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised warm-up.
Each player completes selected technical assessments covering kicking, handballing, marking and ground-ball work.
Players complete role-appropriate movement assessments covering acceleration, agility, deceleration, repeat effort or aerial capability.
All raw results, test versions and modifications are recorded.
Players receive a recovery break.
The squad completes a tactical assessment covering role execution, field-position decisions or structured team phases.
Teams then complete an integrated match simulation.
Observers code possession quality, contested involvement, off-ball work, communication, transition and positional role execution.
Video is used to verify key actions and uncertain ratings.
Players complete a self-assessment after the practical session.
Coaches check all data before interpreting results.
Results are compared with previous baselines and appropriate role benchmarks.
Each player receives a review containing verified strengths and no more than two development priorities.
Individual development plans are updated.
Coaches review the reliability, efficiency and usefulness of every test used.
Tests that do not produce reliable or actionable information are modified or removed from future batteries.
coachingPoints: Use only tests appropriate to the players and purpose.
Standardise instructions, equipment and conditions.
Preserve raw data.
Record invalid and modified attempts clearly.
Separate decision quality from execution.
Interpret physical results with football performance.
Use multiple observations before reaching conclusions.
Avoid creating one overall player ranking.
Protect player privacy.
Convert every meaningful finding into a coaching or development action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Skill quality under fatigue or pressure.
Agreement between player and coach ratings.
Whether testing results match observed football performance.
Whether the assessment process produces useful training priorities.
Whether any test creates unnecessary load or limited practical value.

commonErrors.error: Every available test is included regardless of purpose.
commonErrors.correction: Select measures linked to age, role and development needs.

commonErrors.error: Players are ranked using one combined score.
commonErrors.correction: Report technical, physical, tactical and match categories separately.

commonErrors.error: Modified tests are compared directly with standard results.
commonErrors.correction: Identify modifications and use appropriate comparisons.

commonErrors.error: Coaches collect data without changing training.
commonErrors.correction: Assign practical actions to every confirmed priority.

commonErrors.error: One match period determines the final assessment.
commonErrors.correction: Use testing, training, video and repeated match evidence.

commonErrors.error: Players receive excessive negative feedback.
commonErrors.correction: Present verified strengths and no more than two priorities.

commonErrors.error: The testing system itself is never reviewed.
commonErrors.correction: Evaluate reliability, efficiency, safety and coaching usefulness.

progressions: Link testing with official match statistics and running data.
Create pathway, senior and masters testing batteries.
Use the complete system at pre-season, mid-season and post-season checkpoints.
regressions: Complete the assessment across multiple sessions.
Compare only with the player’s previous baseline.
successIndicators: Demonstrate identifiable technical, physical and tactical strengths.
Recognise one or two priority development areas.
Contribute to their updated development plan.
Understand the actions required before the next review.
Interpret results in role and match context.
Convert findings into individual and squad training priorities.
Review and improve the assessment system itself.
matchApplication: The final assessment connects isolated skill tests, football-specific movement, tactical understanding and match behaviour. It ensures the Testing and Assessment chapter produces practical coaching decisions, reliable player feedback and measurable development rather than disconnected testing results.
relatedDrills: TA-001 to TA-010 – Foundation Testing and Assessment Battery
TA-011 to TA-020 – Technical and Contest Assessment
TA-021 to TA-040 – Football Movement, Physical and Fatigue Assessment
TA-041 to TA-050 – Match Performance, Observation and Review Assessment
TA-051 to TA-059 – Tactical, Team-System and Development-Plan Assessment
MS-100 – Match Simulation Chapter Final Assessment
